title: Tabataba'i's al-Mizan
hookLine: Allamah Tabataba'i's Shia commentary, explaining verse by verse
tomorrow: when you're new to a hard text, how much help is enough?

cards: Two good options, and you can only pick one: two schools, two jobs, two apartments. The pro-and-con list helps, right up until both columns are long. What you need then isn't more items.

It's a scale, and something steady to weigh against. Allamah Tabataba'i, a Shia scholar of Iran, gave his commentary on the Qur'an the name al-Mizan: the balance. His whole method is a way of weighing.

teach.b: Here's the method. To explain a verse, Tabataba'i sets it beside other verses on the same theme and lets the Qur'an weigh its own meaning: the Qur'an explained by the Qur'an.
His reason comes from the book itself, which calls the Qur'an "an exposition of all things." If it explains all things, he argues, it can explain itself.

Only after that does he add separate discussions: reports from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and from the Imams of his household, the Ahl al-Bayt, then philosophy, history and questions of society, each in its own section, kept from tipping the scale.
Notice something. Two days ago, Ibn Kathir, a Sunni scholar, said the best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an. Tabataba'i, a Shia scholar, built his whole commentary on it.

teach.h: SUNNI AND SHIA: A SHARED FIRST STEP.
teach.b: Different schools, real differences, and a shared first step. And the name points somewhere practical.
The Qur'an says God set up the balance, and asks people not to cheat it. Honest weighing means a fixed reference, and no thumb on the scale for the answer you already wanted. That's the balance.

how: Al-Mizan is studied in Shia seminaries and read by Muslims of other schools as well; its method of setting verse beside verse is used in study circles that read the Qur'an thematically.

Tabataba'i, a Shia scholar, built al-Mizan on it; Ibn Kathir, a Sunni, called it the best way.
al-Mizan puts its discussions of reports, philosophy and history in separate sections
so they don't tip the scale on what the verses say.
Tabataba'i reasons that the Qur'an can't explain itself
he argues the opposite: it calls itself an exposition of all things.

games.q: two friends are fighting over what one line in the group chat meant. you're asked to settle it. what does al-Mizan's method suggest?
o: take the side of the friend you're closer to.
screenshot it and ask strangers online to vote.
read the line against the whole thread around it.
games.why: Tabataba'i weighs a verse against other verses. a line is weighed best against the whole conversation it sits in.

practice: Hold one real choice in mind. Name, in a word, what matters most to you in it. Name the pull most likely to put a thumb on your scale: fear, pride, someone else's opinion.
Then make one quiet plan: when that pull shows up, I'll come back to my word.

wordCard.voice: Tabataba'i's al-Mizan: a Shia commentary that explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an, verse weighed against verse, its name meaning the balance.

orig.note: Arabic: al-mizan, the balance or scale; the name of Tabataba'i's commentary.

carryVoice: For today: the balance, steady, with no thumb on the scale. Commentators, four of six, weighed.
